subject: speech-therapy
intro: Speech and language therapy leads to the communication professions — clinicians who treat speech, language, voice and swallowing, and the educators who train the next generation of them.

roles.title: Speech-Language Pathologists
roles.what: Assess and treat people with speech, language, voice and fluency disorders — selecting alternative communication systems and teaching their use, and working with everyone from toddlers with apraxia to adults with aphasia after stroke.
roles.where: Units 3 to 5 are the core caseload — speech sound disorders, language disorders including aphasia and autism, and fluency, voice and resonance; unit 6's dysphagia covers the swallowing work in hospitals; unit 7's AAC is the alternative systems the O*NET description names.

roles.title: Audiologists
roles.what: Assess and treat people with hearing and related disorders — fitting hearing aids, providing auditory training, and supporting the hearing side of communication for children and adults.
roles.where: Unit 1's audiology basics — anatomy of speech production and the acoustics of speech — is the foundation audiologists build on; unit 2's language development and literacy foundations explain why hearing loss is treated early, and unit 7's AAC links to aided communication.

roles.title: Health Specialties Teachers, Postsecondary
roles.what: Teach courses in health specialties — including therapy fields such as speech-language pathology — in universities and professional programmes, often combining classroom teaching with clinical supervision and research.
roles.where: The full curriculum is the syllabus they deliver: speech and hearing sciences, language development and disorders, fluency and voice, dysphagia assessment, and the evidence-based practice and ethics of unit 7.
